planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a trellis or hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; obovate hoya stores water in its thick leaves and prefers to dry out somewhat between waterings.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a trellis or hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; obovate hoya stores water in its thick leaves and prefers to dry out somewhat between waterings. Large, rounded, thick, waxy leaves are sometimes lightly speckled with silver and grow closely along vigorous, twining vines that climb or trail readily, eventually producing rounded clusters of small, fragrant, pale pink, star-shaped flowers with deep red-pink centers on mature growth. Native to Southeast Asian forests, it is a fast-growing, easy hoya well suited to a beginner, tolerating average indoor humidity and occasional missed waterings better than some finer-leaved hoya species. Provide a moss pole, trellis, or hanging basket for the twining stems, and avoid moving or pruning off flower spurs (peduncles), since the same spur reblooms repeatedly over the years.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; Wayet's hoya trails naturally and looks best allowed to cascade rather than staked upright.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; Wayet's hoya trails naturally and looks best allowed to cascade rather than staked upright. Narrow, pointed, deep green leaves often flush purple-red along the margins in bright light, growing densely along slender, gracefully trailing stems that produce small clusters of dark maroon-red, star-shaped flowers with a sweet fragrance most noticeable in the evening. Native to the Philippines, it is a compact, easy-care hoya well suited to a hanging basket or shelf where its cascading stems can drape freely, and, like other hoyas, it blooms repeatedly from the same short flowering spurs, which should never be removed. Allow the potting mix to dry between waterings and provide bright indirect light for the best leaf color and most reliable flowering.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Prince of Orange philodendron is a compact, self-heading (non-climbing) selection that needs no support or moss pole.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Prince of Orange philodendron is a compact, self-heading (non-climbing) selection that needs no support or moss pole. New leaves emerge a vivid orange-red and pass through peach and yellow-green tones as they mature to deep glossy green, so a single healthy plant displays several leaf colors at once in an eye-catching, ever-changing progression. Its neat, upright, non-vining rosette habit keeps it compact and tidy on a shelf, desk, or tabletop without the sprawl of climbing philodendrons, making it a popular low-maintenance choice for smaller spaces. Provide bright indirect light for the most vivid new-leaf color, and allow the top inch of potting mix to dry between waterings.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole or trellis in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Red Emerald philodendron is a vigorous climber that develops larger leaves when given vertical support.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole or trellis in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Red Emerald philodendron is a vigorous climber that develops larger leaves when given vertical support. Glossy, elongated heart-shaped leaves in rich emerald green are set off by wine-red new growth, petioles, and stems, a classic color combination that made this one of the most widely grown climbing philodendrons since its introduction decades ago. As a true climbing aroid it develops larger, more mature foliage and stronger red coloring when trained up a moss pole or trellis rather than left to trail, and it grows quickly under good indoor light with minimal care. Wipe dust from the glossy leaves periodically, provide bright indirect light for the best stem color, and prune to control length and encourage branching.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Manjula pothos is a patented Indian-bred cultivar that colors best in bright indirect light and tolerates average indoor humidity.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Manjula pothos is a patented Indian-bred cultivar that colors best in bright indirect light and tolerates average indoor humidity. Broad, wavy-edged, heart-shaped leaves carry an intricate, creamy-white and silvery-green marbled variegation with a distinctive ruffled, undulating leaf margin unlike the flatter leaves of other pothos cultivars, giving trailing stems a soft, textured look. Bred and patented in India, it is a relatively slower-growing pothos compared to golden or marble queen, but its bold, high-contrast variegation and wavy texture make it a standout in a hanging basket or trained up a small support. Let the potting mix dry between waterings, provide bright indirect light to sustain the variegation, and trim leggy stems to keep the plant full.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole or trellis in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; spade-leaf philodendron is a vigorous climber that develops its largest, most arrow-shaped leaves when given support to climb.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole or trellis in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; spade-leaf philodendron is a vigorous climber that develops its largest, most arrow-shaped leaves when given support to climb. Long, glossy, elongated arrowhead- or spade-shaped leaves with a distinctive quilted texture and pronounced veining are carried on a robust, fast-growing climbing vine that can quickly cover a moss pole or trellis with bold, tropical foliage. One of the classic old-fashioned philodendrons long grown as an easy, undemanding houseplant, it tolerates average indoor conditions and irregular watering better than many newer collector cultivars, making it a reliable choice for a floor specimen given room to climb. Wipe dust from the large leaves periodically, water when the top inch of soil dries, and provide a sturdy support as the vine matures and its leaves grow larger.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket, or mount on a slab, in bright, indirect light in a loose, fast-draining, orchid-bark-based epiphytic mix; string of nickels is a true epiphyte and rots quickly in dense, moisture-retentive potting soil.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket, or mount on a slab, in bright, indirect light in a loose, fast-draining, orchid-bark-based epiphytic mix; string of nickels is a true epiphyte and rots quickly in dense, moisture-retentive potting soil. Small, round, coin-like succulent leaves are strung closely along thin, wiry, trailing stems, forming a dense curtain of tiny green discs that cascades attractively from a hanging basket or mounted slab, punctuated occasionally by small, inconspicuous pale flowers. Native to Southeast Asian and Pacific rainforest canopies, where it grows attached to tree bark rather than rooted in soil, it stores water in its fleshy leaves and prefers to dry out between waterings rather than sit in consistently moist mix. Provide bright, filtered light and excellent air circulation, and mist occasionally to boost humidity without saturating the roots.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference
